title: Alarms, Fault Context and Maintenance Escalation

content.overview: A technician does not need to diagnose every failure, but must capture useful fault context, complete permitted checks and escalate conditions without repeatedly resetting or masking alarms.

vocabulary.definition: A system indication that a measured or controlled condition met a defined alert or fault condition.
An observed effect of a problem that does not by itself establish the root cause.
Information about what, where, when and under what conditions an equipment problem occurred.

sections.title: An alarm is evidence, not a diagnosis
sections.body: Record the alarm, asset, zone, time, readings, visible symptoms and relevant work context. Similar symptoms can have different causes, so technicians should not declare a root cause without supporting evidence.

sections.title: Create a maintenance-ready escalation
sections.body: Perform only the operator checks allowed by the SOP. A useful escalation describes the asset, location, time, observed condition, alarm or reading, safe action taken and affected production area. If the next step requires servicing or hazardous access, stop and refer it.

workedExamples: A pump alarm and dry zone are documented with asset and location before escalation rather than repeatedly reset.
An abnormal fan sound is reported with time, asset and observed condition before the fan fails completely.
commonMistakes: Resetting an alarm repeatedly to make it disappear.
Writing only 'broken' without asset, time, location or observed condition.
content.practicalApplication: Create a maintenance escalation record from a simulated alarm packet containing equipment identity, controller status, room assignment and worker observations.
content.summary: Good fault reporting converts observations into actionable information. Technicians capture context, complete only permitted checks and escalate unresolved equipment conditions.
